A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same aLTT research. Their text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching wireless experiments moved from the main text to the appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original Half Cheetah policy-selection and wireless resource-allocation experiments, including acquisition-policy and betting-strategy comparisons.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original prompt-selection results on instruction-induction tasks and a quantile-risk policy-selection experiment.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, e-process updates, acquisition mechanisms and stopping rules are retained. Prompt selection instantiates the existing candidate-generation and post-selection framework. The quantile experiment introduces a different reliability criterion but does not specify a revised aLTT update or selection procedure.

E1.justification: Section 5.2 and Appendix B.3 add instruction-induction evaluation, with ten reported tasks covering arithmetic, lexical transformations, semantic comparisons and English–Spanish translation. Appendix B.1.2 adds quantile-based reliability requirements for policy selection. Earlier Half Cheetah and wireless coverage is retained.

E2.justification: LTT and non-adaptive aLTT remain the principal comparators, and the aGRAPA, LBOW, ONS, MaxBet and UnitBet comparison is retained. New prompt and quantile experiments reuse existing comparison methods; cited prompt-engineering and quantile-LTT works are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New prompt protocols specify task-dependent 0–1 loss, error target 0.2, tolerance 0.1, ONS betting and a 2,000-round instruction-length evaluation. They also introduce averaging over tasks with non-empty selected sets and a longest-instruction fallback for empty sets. Quantile testing adds q = 0.1 and a horizon reaching 6,000 rounds. Retained experiments' stated settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B.1.2 tests whether efficient policy discovery persists when reliability concerns quantile risk rather than mean reward. Prompt experiments additionally examine acquisition-policy and accuracy-threshold sensitivity. Existing betting-strategy and wireless analyses remain; task-level score breakdowns alone are not counted as new ablations.

E5.justification: v2 adds shaded bands around the previously line-only TPR curves in Figure 2. Their statistical meaning and underlying run or seed counts remain unspecified. Figure 3 already contained bands in v1, so uncertainty displays are expanded rather than introduced throughout the paper for the first time.

E6.justification: Figures 4–5 and 11–12 add aggregate and task-level prompt-discovery and instruction-length results. Figure 7 adds quantile-risk results showing approximately 0.7 TPR for strongly adaptive acquisition versus zero for LTT. These are new experimental findings, not improvements under the earlier mean-reward setting. Earlier wireless and betting-strategy results are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1.2 introduces the quantile-risk definition in Equation 21 and discusses reversing inequalities for rewards. Appendix A.2.3 corrects the eBH explanation from larger to smaller thresholds for smaller e-values. The existing e-process equations and principal guarantees remain unchanged; no new proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement replace wireless engineering with automated prompt engineering as the second highlighted application. LLM calibration changes from a proposed future direction to a demonstrated application. The central claims of adaptive testing, statistical validity and testing efficiency remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets broader reliable-prompt discovery as enabling shorter instructions and lower processing cost, and explains how stricter accuracy requirements affect instruction length. It also motivates quantile risk through safety and explains choosing minimum e-value merging for simplicity. Existing distribution-shift and simulation-aided extensions remain.

D1.justification: The prompt application specifies Llama3 8B Instruct as the target model, Llama3.3 70B Instruct as the candidate generator, forward-generation prompting and ONS betting. These are concrete implementation disclosures for the added experiment. Existing RL and wireless implementation information is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused literature on automated prompt engineering, instruction induction, Llama models, quantile risk and e-value merging, while removing several earlier general hyperparameter examples. Its central positioning relative to LTT, conformal risk control and sequential e-process testing remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Parts of the motivation and contribution narrative are rewritten around prompt selection, former Section 5.2 moves to Appendix B.2, and Sangwoo Park is added to the author list. Most methodological prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned around prompt generation, five new result figures are added, and retained wireless displays move to Figures 8–10 in the appendix. Figure 2 gains shaded bands. Typography, running headers, algorithm formatting and figure placement also change substantially.

improvement.justification: The prompt experiments provide useful evidence for costly LLM evaluation, while the quantile experiment tests a different reliability objective. Task-level plots make the new findings easier to assess, earlier evidence remains available, and the eBH explanation is corrected. The gains are limited by undefined uncertainty bands and incomplete reproducibility details for the added experiments.
